newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council still divided on Iraqi resolution.
newsitem.headline: UN Council still divided on Iraqi resolution.

text.p: The Security Council on Wednesday was split on a proposal to condemn Iraq for its offensive in the north, with Britain hoping for agreement shortly but Russia saying the two sides were still far apart.
"We cannot support the latest version of the British draft," said Russia's ambassador Sergei Lavrov in reference to British proposals before the council.
He hinted that Moscow might abstain if no compromise could be found before the draft is put to a vote.
But British envoy Stephen Gomersall, who drafted the text, had already revised it substantially to meet objections from Russia, France, China and others and expected a vote on Thursday.
"I think by the end of the day we will have support for the draft resolution that we put forth," he said, adding: "I think you find that we will have solid agreement by Thursday."
The current council president, Ambassador Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau, also said substantial progress had been made in "bridging the gap" and that the council could vote late on Thursday.
At issue was whether Iraq should be condemned outright, with Lavrov insisting that Baghdad's troops invaded their own territory at the request of one Kurdish party.
The three northern provinces have been under allied protection since the end of the Gulf War when President Saddam Hussein put down a rebellion and strafed fleeing Kurdish civilians from the air.

But the British draft made no mention of the American cruise missiles blasting Iraqi targets in southern Iraq in response to Baghdad's attacks in the north, presumably because the council was divided on the issue and because U.N. resolutions did not authorise the use of force in this case.
The draft condemns Iraq's operations in the northern city or Arbit and "expresses grave concern" about a wider escalation of hostilities in the region. It demands Iraqi troops withdraw immediately.
It also calls for talks among feuding Kurdish parties, with France saying Iraq needed to be involved in those negotiations and others opposed.

And at the insistence of several countries, the British resolution no longer poses any conditions for the implementation of an oil-for-food deal as the United States wanted. Instead it deletes any reference to it, with members agreeing to discuss that controversy separately.
Said one French envoy: "We don't want the plan dependent on events in Iraq only and add new conditions to it. Many agree that the situation in the north is now different than it was in 1991."
Under the oil-for-food plan Iraq can export $2 billion worth of petroleum to buy food and medicine for its people suffering under sanctions since Bagdad's troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Even before two U.S. cruise missile attacks, Boutros-Ghali said on Sunday he was delaying the arrival of U.N. monitors needed to supervise the agreement becuase of fears for their safety.
There is also a division in the council among non-aligned council members with Chile and Honduras favouring the British draft and Egypt and Indonesia voicing strong reservations.
